state.question: Why do the four measurement streams (pendulum_lab, pendulum_obs, resonator_lab, resonator_obs) show near-zero or negative cross-correlations at various time offsets, when instruments measuring the same physical quantity should co-vary positively?

hypotheses.label: Instrumental independence: each stream measures a genuinely distinct physical quantity or aspect, not the same phenomenon
hypotheses.rationale: The cross-checks show that pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs (nominally both measuring pendulum periods) correlate at only 0.232, well within chance noise (±0.529). Similarly, the two resonator streams correlate at 0.384, just barely above chance. Even 'lab' vs 'obs' pairs show negative or weak correlations. If all four instruments were measuring stable properties of the same system, I would expect consistent positive covariance. Instead, the pattern suggests either (a) the observational methods or environments differ enough to produce decorrelated readouts, or (b) the instruments are sensing different degrees of freedom. This is the most parsimonious explanation that requires no exotic physics.

hypotheses.label: Systematic drift or non-stationarity in one or more instruments, masking true correlations
hypotheses.rationale: With only 10 days of baseline data, genuine slow drifts (longer than ~5 day timescale) would not yet be visible in level-change analysis. If pendulum_lab is drifting upward while resonator_obs drifts downward, their cross-correlation would be suppressed. The 'echoes' analysis (readings matching their own lag-8 or lag-7 values) shows all near-zero or weakly negative correlations, which is suspicious—true periodic drift should produce positive echoes. However, the lack of clear level changes and the fact that 'echoes' are all weak (within or near chance) argues against strong drift.
